title: Their children
hookLine: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and sons who died in infancy

cards: Abu al-Qasim. Father of Qasim. It's a kunya, a name built from a child's name, a way of calling a man through his child.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was called by this one, and it is still used of him today. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even has him say: call yourselves by my name, but not by my kunya. And Qasim himself?
A little boy who did not live to grow up. His father carried his name anyway.

teach.h: SONS WHO DID NOT GROW UP.
teach.b: Ibn Ishaq lists the children Khadijah bore him. Sons first: al-Qasim, then the names al-Tayyib and al-Tahir, the good one and the pure one.
Some scholars read those two names as one son, called Abdullah, with two titles; the sources don't settle it. Ibn Ishaq says simply that the sons died before Islam came.
Then the daughters, each with her own story still ahead: Zaynab. Ruqayyah. Umm Kulthum.
Fatimah. Ibn Ishaq says they lived to see Islam, accepted it, and emigrated with their father. Here traditions read the record in more than one way.

teach.h: FOUR DAUGHTERS, AND HOW THEY'RE READ.
teach.b: Sunni tradition counts all four as daughters of the Prophet and Khadijah.
Some Shia scholars hold that Fatimah alone was their daughter by birth, and that the others were raised in the house; other Shia scholars accept all four.

teach.h: FATIMAH IS A PART OF ME.
teach.b: And of Fatimah, her father says in Sahih al-Bukhari: Fatimah is a part of me. Put it together and the house in Mecca comes into view: a mother who traded, a father who was trusted, girls growing up, and small graves too.
Grief came into that home before any revelation. And the sources keep every name, even the boys who died small. One more picture, from a long dream the Prophet describes in Sahih al-Bukhari.
He sees the prophet Ibrahim in a garden, and around him, children. He's told they are the children who died young.

how: Muslims who lose a child say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un and pray for the family; the Prophet's ﷺ name Abu al-Qasim, after a son who died young, is still used of him today.

games.q: your little son has died. people will call you by a name for the rest of your life. which one do you keep?
o: a name with no child in it.
father of the son who died.
father of a daughter who lived.
games.why: he was known as Abu al-Qasim, father of Qasim, the boy who did not grow up. the grief stayed in his name.

practice: Go gently; if this is close to you, take only what you can.
Bring to mind a child who didn't get to grow up, one you knew, one in your family's story, or one you only heard about, and say the name if you know it; if you don't, the child is still held.
If you pray, ask Allah's mercy for that child and comfort for those who miss them; if not, simply keep the name, or the face, in mind.

wordCard.voice: Their children. Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah, and the sons who died small, al-Qasim among them, whose name his father carried. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: father of Qasim, the Prophet's kunya, taken from his son's name.

carryVoice: Your line: every child remembered. Even the smallest has a name on the page. See you tomorrow.
